title: Net Worth: What You Own Minus What You Owe

contentBlocks.content: What is net worth?
Net worth is a snapshot of your financial position. It compares the value of what you own with the amount you owe.
Net worth = Assets − Liabilities

contentBlocks.title: The simple idea
contentBlocks.content: Add up what you own, add up what you owe, and subtract what you owe from what you own.
Assets: what you own

An asset is something you own that has financial value. Depending on your situation, assets can include cash, savings accounts, investments, retirement accounts, property, business interests, and other valuable possessions.
Not every asset is equally useful

Two assets can have the same financial value while providing very different levels of access, income, risk, or usefulness. A savings account is immediately accessible, while a property may take time to sell.
Liabilities: what you owe
Liabilities are debts and financial obligations you owe to other people or organizations. Examples include credit-card balances, personal loans, student loans, auto loans, mortgages, and other debts.
A simple example

contentBlocks.title: Starting with two numbers
contentBlocks.content: Suppose you have $40,000 in assets and $15,000 in liabilities.
Your net worth is $25,000.
Build your personal balance sheet
A simple personal balance sheet lists your assets on one side and your liabilities on the other. This gives you the information needed to calculate net worth.
Step 1: List your assets
Start with the financial value of things you own. Use reasonable current values rather than what you originally paid.

contentBlocks.title: Example asset list
contentBlocks.content: Savings: $8,000. Investments: $12,000. Car: $15,000. Property equity-related value before debt: $100,000.
Step 2: List your liabilities
Next, list outstanding debts and other financial obligations.

contentBlocks.title: Example liability list
contentBlocks.content: Credit-card debt: $2,000. Car loan: $7,000. Mortgage: $60,000.
Step 3: Subtract liabilities from assets
In this example, net worth is $66,000.
A house does not automatically equal its full value in your net worth
If you own a property worth $300,000 but still owe $220,000 on the mortgage, the property contributes $80,000 of equity to your net worth.
Equity is the part you actually own
Equity is the value of an asset after subtracting the debt attached to it. It is especially useful when thinking about financed assets such as homes and cars.
Equity = Asset value − Debt secured against the asset

contentBlocks.title: Car equity
contentBlocks.content: If a car is worth $25,000 and you owe $10,000 on the car loan, your equity in the car is $15,000.
Net worth can be positive
Positive net worth means your assets are worth more than your liabilities.

contentBlocks.title: Positive net worth
contentBlocks.content: Assets of $80,000 and liabilities of $30,000 produce a net worth of $50,000.
Net worth can also be zero
If your assets and liabilities have the same value, your net worth is zero.

contentBlocks.title: Zero net worth
contentBlocks.content: Assets of $50,000 and liabilities of $50,000 result in zero net worth.
Net worth can be negative
Negative net worth means you owe more than the value of what you own. This can happen for many reasons, including high debt, education costs, business losses, or having few assets.

contentBlocks.title: Negative net worth
contentBlocks.content: Suppose you have $20,000 in assets but owe $35,000.
Your net worth would be negative $15,000.
Negative net worth is information, not a permanent identity
A negative number does not mean you are financially hopeless. It tells you that, at that point in time, your liabilities exceed your assets. That information can help you decide what needs attention.
Net worth is a snapshot
Your net worth can change from month to month because of saving, debt repayment, investment movements, property values, business values, and other changes.
Cash flow and net worth are different

Net worth tells you about your financial position at a point in time. Cash flow tells you what money comes in and goes out during a period. A person can have high net worth but poor monthly cash flow, or modest net worth with healthy monthly cash flow.
Liquidity matters too
Liquidity describes how easily an asset can be converted into money without a major loss in value. Cash is highly liquid. A property is generally much less liquid.

contentBlocks.title: Important distinction
contentBlocks.content: Net worth tells you how much financial value you have after liabilities. It does not tell you how much cash you can access today.
A high net worth does not always mean easy access to cash

contentBlocks.title: Asset-rich, cash-poor
contentBlocks.content: Someone may own a property worth $500,000 with little debt but have only $2,000 in readily available cash. Their net worth may be substantial, but they could still struggle with an immediate $5,000 emergency.
Track net worth over time
Calculating net worth once can be useful, but tracking it periodically can reveal whether your overall financial position is moving in the direction you want.

contentBlocks.title: Tracking progress
contentBlocks.content: Suppose your net worth is $25,000 today and $31,000 one year later.
Your net worth increased by $6,000 during that period. The reason for the increase could include saving, debt repayment, asset growth, or a combination of factors.
Debt repayment can increase net worth
Paying down debt can improve net worth because the liability becomes smaller. You do not necessarily need to buy a new asset for your net worth to improve.

contentBlocks.title: Debt repayment
contentBlocks.content: If your assets remain at $50,000 while your debt falls from $30,000 to $20,000, your net worth increases from $20,000 to $30,000.
Saving can increase net worth
When you add money to your savings and do not add an equal liability, your assets increase and your net worth can increase.

contentBlocks.title: Adding savings
contentBlocks.content: If your assets increase from $30,000 to $35,000 while liabilities remain at $10,000, your net worth rises from $20,000 to $25,000.
Borrowing can make an asset and liability rise together
When you borrow money to buy an asset, the asset and liability can increase at the same time. That means the transaction does not automatically create the same amount of new net worth.

contentBlocks.title: Buying with borrowed money
contentBlocks.content: Suppose you borrow $20,000 to purchase an asset worth $20,000. Your assets increase by $20,000, but your liabilities also increase by $20,000.
Ignoring fees and other factors, the transaction itself does not increase net worth at the moment of purchase.
Why net worth is useful
Net worth can help you see whether your financial resources are growing relative to your obligations. It can also reveal whether debt is consuming a large part of your financial position.
But net worth is not the only number that matters
A healthy financial picture also considers income, cash flow, emergency savings, debt costs, liquidity, financial goals, and the risks surrounding your assets.
Common misconceptions
Misconception: Net worth means how much cash you have
Reality: Net worth includes assets beyond cash and subtracts liabilities. You can have substantial net worth without having the same amount available in your bank account.
Misconception: Owning a $300,000 home means your net worth increased by $300,000
Reality: If the home was purchased with debt, the liability must be considered. The relevant contribution to net worth is affected by the home's value and the debt attached to it.
Misconception: Negative net worth means you are a failure
Reality: Net worth is a financial measurement, not a judgment of your personal worth. A negative number can be a starting point for making informed decisions.
Misconception: Net worth should always increase every month
Reality: Net worth can fluctuate because asset values change and financial circumstances change. What matters is understanding the reasons behind changes and looking at the longer-term direction.
Misconception: You need expensive assets to have wealth

Reality: Wealth can be built through many forms of assets and consistent financial decisions. The value comes from the overall financial position, not from how impressive an individual possession looks.

contentBlocks.title: Build a simple balance sheet
contentBlocks.content: Imagine you have $10,000 in savings, $20,000 in investments, a car worth $18,000, and $8,000 of debt. Calculate your net worth before moving on.
Use net worth to improve decisions
The purpose of tracking net worth is not to compete with other people. Use it to understand your own financial direction and make better decisions.

contentBlocks.title: Decision moment
contentBlocks.content: If two choices have similar lifestyles but one leaves you with more assets, less debt, and greater financial flexibility, which choice is more likely to strengthen your long-term financial position?

Net worth is the value of what you own minus what you owe. Assets increase the number, while liabilities reduce it. Net worth can be positive, zero, or negative, and it can change over time through saving, debt repayment, asset movements, and other financial changes. It is useful, but it should be considered alongside cash flow and liquidity.

contentBlocks.title: Remember
contentBlocks.content: Do not ask only, 'What do I own?' Ask, 'What do I own, what do I owe, and what is the difference?'

quizzes.question: What is the basic formula for net worth?
quizzes.explanation: Net worth is calculated by subtracting liabilities from assets.

quizzes.question: You have $40,000 in assets and $15,000 in liabilities. What is your net worth?
A property is worth $300,000 and you owe $220,000 on it. What is the property equity?
What does negative net worth mean?
options: You owe more than the value of what you own
You have no assets at all
quizzes.explanation: Negative net worth occurs when liabilities exceed assets.

quizzes.question: You have $80,000 in assets and $30,000 in liabilities. What is your net worth?
Net worth tells you exactly how much cash you can access today.
quizzes.explanation: Net worth includes assets that may not be immediately liquid, such as property.

quizzes.question: If your assets stay at $50,000 while your debt falls from $30,000 to $20,000, what happens to your net worth?
quizzes.explanation: Net worth rises from $20,000 to $30,000, an increase of $10,000.

quizzes.question: You have $10,000 in savings, $20,000 in investments, a car worth $18,000, and $8,000 in debt. What is your net worth?
Why can someone have high net worth but still struggle with an immediate expense?
options: Net worth can include assets that are not easily accessible as cash
High net worth means you cannot own cash
Net worth always equals bank balance
quizzes.explanation: A large portion of net worth may be tied up in less-liquid assets.

quizzes.question: What is the best reason to track your net worth?
options: To prove that you look wealthy
To understand your financial direction and make better decisions
quizzes.explanation: Net worth is most useful as a tool for understanding and improving your own financial position.
